subject: Vectorization, matrix and vector notation, and related issues

messages.author: 4cef6eb14d12f9f6
messages.subject: Vectorization, matrix and vector notation, and related issues
parts:
I have a super slow model that I think would benefit from vectorization, but in spite of reading the relevant pages of the user's manual and reading related posts on this group, I can't figure it out. The answers are there, in language a sixth-grader can understand, but evidently I need them explained in language a third-grader can understand. 

I am not sure about how 
real X[n,m];
differs from
vector[n] x[m];
or why I would prefer one of these over the other.

Also, if I am working with X[n,m,p], can I use statements like
X[n,m] ~ student_t(4,z,sigma) 
where z is a vector of length p? That is, is X[i,j] the vector obtained by evaluating X[i,j,k] for k from 1:p?

And what if I want to access that middle index rather than the last one, is there a way to do that? That is, can I specify the first and last indices somehow, and get all values of that middle one as a vector, the equivalent of X[3,j,5] where j runs from 1:m?

To take the babiest of baby steps first, I have code like this that I would like to vectorize (note that beta_TOD has three indices, and beta_TOD_1 has only two): 

transformed parameters{
  real delta_TOD_1[n_weeks,n_DayTimes]; // change in TOD effects wkdays
  real delta_TOD_2[n_weeks,n_DayTimes]; // change in TOD effects wkends 
  for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
    for (i_dt in 1:n_DayTimes) { 
      // change from one week to the next, at a given time
      delta_TOD_1[i_wk,i_dt] <- beta_TOD[1,i_wk,i_dt]-beta_TOD[1,i_wk-1,i_dt];
      delta_TOD_2[i_wk,i_dt] <- beta_TOD[2,i_wk,i_dt]-beta_TOD[2,i_wk-1,i_dt];
}      
model {
  for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
    for (i_dt in 1:n_DayTimes) {
      delta_TOD_1[i_wk,i_dt] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma);
      delta_TOD_2[i_wk,i_dt] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma);   
    }
  }
}

Can I replace the loops with statements like
for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
  delta_TOD_1[i_wk] <- beta_TOD[1,i_wk]-beta_TOD[1,i_wk-1];
}
for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
  delta_TOD_1[iwk] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma);
}
 
I fear you're going to say "just look at p. 75 of the 1.1.0 manual and it explains all this", and all I can say to that is: I need to be treated like a third grader on this, seriously. I see that you have changed x[K,N] to vector[K] x[N] for example, but I don't know if that is necessary or merely a convenience, and if it's necessary I don't know how to tell when it's necessary, and I really _really_ don't know the difference between vector[] and row_vector[].

I'd appreciate any help you can offer.

--Phil

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vectorization, matrix and vector notation, and related issues
parts:
On 2/1/13 1:32 PM, Phil Price wrote:
> I have a super slow model that I think would benefit from vectorization, but in spite of reading the relevant pages of
> the user's manual and reading related posts on this group, I can't figure it out. The answers are there, in language a
> sixth-grader can understand, but evidently I need them explained in language a third-grader can understand.
>
> I am not sure about how
> real X[n,m];
> differs from
> vector[n] x[m];
> or why I would prefer one of these over the other.

X is declared as an (n x m)-array.

x is declared as an m-array of n-vectors. The
array indices come first when using an array of
vectors or matrices.

You've declared them in opposite orders. So you'd loop
like this:

for (i in 1:n) {
for (j in 1:m) {
X[i] or row(X,i) is a size m row vector
col(X,j) is a size n column vector
X[i,j] is of type real
x[j] is a size n vector *** most efficient ***
x[j,i] is of type real
}
}

If you use vector or matrix operations, they need to
be declared as vectors. It's more efficient to pull
a subarray out than a submatrix, but I wouldn't worry
too much about that. If nothing gets vectorized, the
array versions seem to be easier for people to understand.

> Also, if I am working with X[n,m,p], can I use statements like
> X[n,m] ~ student_t(4,z,sigma)
> where z is a vector of length p? That is, is X[i,j] the vector obtained by evaluating X[i,j,k] for k from 1:p?

Yes, as long as X is declared as

real X[n,m,p];

or

vector[p] X[n,m];

> And what if I want to access that middle index rather than the last one, is there a way to do that?
> That is, can I
> specify the first and last indices somehow, and get all values of that middle one as a vector, the equivalent of
> X[3,j,5] where j runs from 1:m?

No. Adding full R- or MATLAB-like matrix slicing
is on our to-do list.

> To take the babiest of baby steps first, I have code like this that I would like to vectorize (note that beta_TOD has
> three indices, and beta_TOD_1 has only two):
>
> transformed parameters{
> real delta_TOD_1[n_weeks,n_DayTimes]; // change in TOD effects wkdays
> real delta_TOD_2[n_weeks,n_DayTimes]; // change in TOD effects wkends
> for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
> for (i_dt in 1:n_DayTimes) {
> // change from one week to the next, at a given time
> delta_TOD_1[i_wk,i_dt] <- beta_TOD[1,i_wk,i_dt]-beta_TOD[1,i_wk-1,i_dt];
> delta_TOD_2[i_wk,i_dt] <- beta_TOD[2,i_wk,i_dt]-beta_TOD[2,i_wk-1,i_dt];
> }
> model {
> for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
> for (i_dt in 1:n_DayTimes) {
> delta_TOD_1[i_wk,i_dt] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma);
> delta_TOD_2[i_wk,i_dt] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma);
> }
> }
> }
>
> Can I replace the loops with statements like
> for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
> delta_TOD_1[i_wk] <- beta_TOD[1,i_wk]-beta_TOD[1,i_wk-1];
> }

No. You can only do matrix/vector operations like subtraction on vectors.
So you'd need beta_TOD[1,i_wk] and beta_tod[1,i_wk-1] to
be the same vector or matrix type as delta_TOD_1[i_wk].

So your declarations should be:

vector[n_DayTimes] delta_TOD_1[n_weeks];
vector[n_DayTimes] delta_TOD_2[n_weeks];

Then everything will work. The I/O won't change because
the indexing order is the same as the array declaration.

The following would've worked with your array declarations
and will also work with the vector declartations.

> for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
> delta_TOD_1[iwk] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma);
> }

> I fear you're going to say "just look at p. 75 of the 1.1.0 manual and it explains all this", and all I can say to that

We're trying to be a little more helpful than that!

It also helps us to see where people aren't getting the
explanations in our manual. If you finally figure it out,
it's even more helpful to us if you give us some hint as
to how to make the manual more helpful.

> is: I need to be treated like a third grader on this, seriously. I see that you have changed x[K,N] to vector[K] x[N]
> for example, but I don't know if that is necessary or merely a convenience, and if it's necessary I don't know how to
> tell when it's necessary, and I really _really_ don't know the difference between vector[] and row_vector[].

Read the manual section on "Arithmetic and Matrix Expressions".
It contains everything you need to know :-)

I'm not sure what you mean by "vector[]" and "row_vector[]". That's
not legal syntax anywhere in Stan.

The difference between the vector type and row_vector type is that
the first is a column vector and the second is a row vector :-)
The reason this matters is that if you declare

row_vector[K] x;
vector[K] y;

then (x * y) is of type real (we infer the simplest type),
whereas (y * x) is of type matrix. Also, if m is a matrix,
then row(m,i) returns a row vector and col(m,j) a vector.

In may places, you can use row vectors and vectors interchangeably.
> I'd appreciate any help you can offer.

And do let us know if this is still not clear enough to work
from.

A good strategy to figure these things out on your own is
to try very simple test cases with just the behavior you're
curious about.

- Bob

I'm a big fan of doing toy problems in order to learn, but I find that I quickly grow frustrated if I don't have a certain base level of understanding. I don't mind failing two or three times if I'll eventually get it, but my mindset is different if I fear that no matter how many times I try I might not succeed due to some missing bit of information or insight. Just an update.  

I now know enough to make most of my code work as desired, but I'm still perplexed about a few things. For example, I have data structures from which I can access individual elements with
delta_TOD_1[i_wk, i_dt] and beta_TOD[k,i_wk,i_dt]

I can create these structures one of two ways: 
(1) I can use declarations like
real delta_TOD_1[n_weeks,n_DayTimes]
or 
(2) I can use statements like
vector [n_DayTimes] delta_TOD_1[n_weeks]

I am not sure why these are not functionally equivalent, but they're not: if I want to make statements like the one below to do vectorwise operations, then only form (2) will work, form (1) generates an error (i.e. does not parse).
for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {

delta_TOD_1[i_wk] <- beta_TOD[1,i_wk]-beta_TOD[1,i_dt];
}

I thought that with either form of declaration, beta_TOD[1,4], say, would be a vector of length n_DayTimes, but evidently this is not the case?

I can do most of what I want simply by using form (2) above, so I'm OK for now except for not understanding why form (1) doesn't work. But I'll also need to extract other rows or columns from these data structures (which I think of as arrays, although I assume the whole issue is that they are not in fact stored the same was as the arrays in form (1)), so I hope I'm not robbing Peter to pay Paul as far as time savings goes. I guess I'll find out eventually. 

No action item here for you, just letting you know that somehow, in spite of your best efforts, I do not understand the distinction between these data structures! Embarrassing but true.

On 2/2/13 6:29 PM, Phil Price wrote:
> Just an update.
>
> I now know enough to make most of my code work as desired, but I'm still perplexed about a few things. For example, I
> have data structures from which I can access individual elements with
> delta_TOD_1[i_wk, i_dt] and beta_TOD[k,i_wk,i_dt]
>
> I can create these structures one of two ways:
> (1) I can use declarations like
> real delta_TOD_1[n_weeks,n_DayTimes]
> or
> (2) I can use statements like
> vector [n_DayTimes] delta_TOD_1[n_weeks]
>
> I am not sure why these are not functionally equivalent,

(1) declares a 2D array of reals

(2) declareds a 1D array of real vectors

They are indexed the same way, but delta_TOD_1[i] is
a (column) vector, and so can be used in vector
arithmetic.

> but they're not: if I want to make statements like the one
> below to do vectorwise operations, then only form (2) will work, form (1) generates an error (i.e. does not parse).
>
> for (i_wk in 2:n_weeks) {
> delta_TOD_1[i_wk] <- beta_TOD[1,i_wk]-beta_TOD[1,i_dt];
> }
Right.

> I thought that with either form of declaration, beta_TOD[1,4], say, would be a vector of length n_DayTimes, but
> evidently this is not the case?
Right. See above.

> I can do most of what I want simply by using form (2) above, so I'm OK for now except for not understanding why form (1)
> doesn't work.

You need to understand that every expression comes with a type.
The operations defined in the index are all typed and they only
apply to arguments of the appropriate type. There are no arithmetic
operations defined over arrays.

> But I'll also need to extract other rows or columns from these data structures (which I think of as
> arrays, although I assume the whole issue is that they are not in fact stored the same was as the arrays in form (1)),
> so I hope I'm not robbing Peter to pay Paul as far as time savings goes. I guess I'll find out eventually.

They're not stored in the same way. Each is more
efficient for different operations. But having said
that, it's not something that'll make a measurable
difference in a model of any complexity because the
gradient calculations will dominate.

> No action item here for you, just letting you know that somehow, in spite of your best efforts, I do not understand the
> distinction between these data structures! Embarrassing but true.

Thanks for sharing.

The key is understanding typed programming languages
in which every expression has a type.

So if I write a * b + c, there are four subexpressions:

a * b
a
b
c

You can work bottom up from the subexpressions to see
what the type of the result is.

Programs have to be well typed.

- Bob
